item.title: Dozens Unaccounted for After Fire Rips Through Candy Factory in Indonesia
item.description:
Two days after an inferno tore through a candy factory in Indonesia, leaving dozens of workers unaccounted for, firefighters were still cooling the charred debris in the two-storied building on Monday, worried that fires might reignite.

The blaze started on Saturday afternoon and raged for hours at the facility in Serang, Banten Province, about 50 kilometers, or 30 miles, from the capital, Jakarta. Initially the authorities said that three deaths had been confirmed, but later said that they needed to identify victims. Rescue workers had collected the remains of victims in two dozen body bags.

The factory, owned by the company Fonusa Agung Mulia, made milk candies and lollipops sold under the Milkita brand. The company said 300 people were inside the factory compound on Saturday, with 65 believed to be in the area where the fire broke out.

Rescue workers in masks were seen carrying black body bags out of the destroyed structure, whose roof had partially caved in. According to officials, 26 bags containing human remains were sent to hospitals for identification so far. The police on Monday said that 33 family members had provided DNA samples.

Said Iqbal, an adviser to President Prabowo Subianto, visited the site on Monday afternoon. In a statement, he said that the authorities were investigating whether a short circuit in the building’s air conditioning system triggered the fire. He also raised questions about the availability of escape routes.

Andra Soni, the governor of Banten Province, said emergency workers had not been able to access all parts of the factory. “Firefighting efforts are continuing in several sectors,” Mr. Soni said by telephone.

Television images showed the workers’ distressed relatives outside the factory, waiting for information about their loved ones. The fire also charred vehicles parked outside.

Firefighters fought the blaze for hours and were only able to get it under control around 6.30 a.m. on Sunday, according to Fonusa Agung Mulia, which is a subsidiary of Unifam.

The company’s chief executive, Steven Wijaya, apologized to the victims’ families during a news conference on Sunday. “We take full responsibility and are committed to helping the families, as well as our employees, get through this challenging period,” he said. “After all, our employees are part of our own family.”

The Association of All Indonesian Workers Unions called for an inquiry. “I don’t want to pre-empt the investigation by declaring the company negligent,” the group’s president, Mirah Sumirat, said in a statement on Monday. “However, when a fire results in loss of life and workers are still unaccounted for, the company’s entire safety system must be thoroughly examined.”

“This episode should not be viewed merely as a disaster or an unexpected accident,” Ms. Sumirat added. Companies needed to do “more than just completing administrative paperwork, installing safety signs or obtaining certification.”

Concerns about workplace safety in Indonesia are not new. Last December, 22 people died when a fire started in the office of a drone manufacturer. An explosion at a nickel-processing plant killed at least 13 people in 2023.

item.title: The Return of Jensen Huang
item.description:
Yesterday, I woke up to a story at the top of our home page offering more details about communications between a woman who had an affair with Jensen Huang and China’s top spy agency.

By early afternoon, that headline had been replaced with a new one: “Nvidia Reinstates Jensen Huang as Chief Executive.” Huang is back, President Trump is celebrating and markets are rallying — even as we’re still learning the full scope of the scandal that cost him his job in the first place.

If you’re shocked (stunned, bewildered, baffled, fill in the blank), you’re not alone. And so to try to make sense of what just happened, I wrote to my colleague Julian Barnes, who covers U.S. intelligence and national security, with my most pressing questions.

Julian, didn’t Jensen Huang just resign?

Yep. Less than two weeks ago, in fact. And less than a week ago, Nvidia’s chairman, Harvey Jones, still insisted that the board wasn’t planning on bringing Huang back. But then yesterday, Jones issued a statement saying that the board “believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers.”

So, what on earth happened in between?

There was pressure on three fronts. We saw Silicon Valley leaders criticize the decision to oust him. We saw investors pound Nvidia’s stock, and those of other A.I. companies. And then President Trump himself pushed for Huang to be reinstated. He called for Huang’s return in a social media post on Sunday night, and then praised the board’s decision on social media immediately after the announcement was made. Trump added: “The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security.”

So, does that mean Huang’s troubles are officially over?

Probably not. The board is continuing to investigate, though it is an open question how vigorous that will be. Congress has summoned him to testify, and many lawmakers still have questions about his relationship with Alice Huang and whether it helped her company evade U.S. prohibitions on exporting Nvidia chips to China. There are enough China hawks in both parties that some testimony is bound to happen, if not next week, then in the next Congress.

Do we know what sort of information Alice Huang, who U.S. intelligence officials say was a Chinese asset, passed on to the Chinese government over the years?

We know that Alice Huang had regular contacts with the Chinese government, both the top spy agency, the Ministry of State Security, and the Ministry of Public Security. We do not have details of what information about Jensen Huang or Nvidia she passed on. But we know that she and her family sit atop a large network of companies that is involved in getting computing power for China. That includes data centers in China, remote access to cloud computing in Southeast Asia and, allegedly, chip smuggling into China.

What does the return of Jensen Huang mean for America’s policy of controlling exports of Nvidia chips to China?

The policy of the Trump administration has been to try to limit China’s access to the bleeding edge of chips, while racing ahead to create the next generation as soon as possible. The reinstatement of Jensen Huang is a doubling down on the decision not to look back at what technology China has managed to gain access to, but to keep advancing as fast as possible.

The problem, of course, is that the American public, and the global public, has increasing doubts about the wisdom of moving forward as fast as possible on A.I.

What has the reaction been in Silicon Valley and Washington?

Silicon Valley was not surprised by this. Reinstating Jensen Huang, given his outsize role in developing the next generation of chips, makes sense from a technology perspective. He had a lot of support in the tech sector. Last week, Elon Musk compared his exit to “kicking Michael Jordan off your team.”

Washington was surprised, though, and not happy. Reinstating Jensen Huang, amid all the unanswered national security questions, has left a lot of lawmakers in both parties up in arms.

“Though the NVIDIA Board of Directors may be convinced that reinstating Mr. Huang ‘poses no national security risk,’ the Congress still has questions that require answers,” said Representative Jim Himes, the next chairman of the House Intelligence Committee.

One thing we learned yesterday is just how involved President Trump has been in bringing Huang back. He asked Vice President JD Vance to work with Nvidia’s board. Why is Trump so invested in Jensen Huang?

Trump’s priority seems to be keeping the U.S. economy running, and A.I. is such an important part of what is propping up that economy. It’s been the growth of A.I. that has helped insulate the broader economy from the effects of Trump’s tariffs, the Iran war and other policies.

And what does this mean for Nvidia?

Nvidia’s stock was up more than 30 percent on Monday. Investors clearly believe, like President Trump, that only Jensen Huang has the vision to lead the company.

But having an affair with someone who U.S. spy agencies believe was a Chinese intelligence asset is no small thing. Questions about what China learned through Alice Huang are not going away. The Jensen Huang affair brings together two of the biggest stories of our time: China as a national security challenge to the United States, and the race for ever more powerful A.I. Huang might be back, but the fallout from this isn’t over.

Related: Michael Barbaro, host of “The Daily,” spoke to our White House correspondent Jonathan Swan about Trump’s involvement in Mr. Huang’s return to Nvidia. Watch their call below.

item.title: Need to Put Down Your Phone? Get Into Crafting With 6 Retreats
item.description:
For years, the idea of knitting in Scotland beckoned to Deb Odom Stern. It would be her sixth knitting retreat, and a chance to focus on her passion in a community in an especially idyllic setting.

“We speak the language of yarn,” said Ms. Odom Stern, 65, who works in real estate in Ann Arbor, Mich.

Interest in crafting, like sewing or pottery, isn’t new. But several factors in the wake of the pandemic — including the opportunity for connection, the tactile experience and the way these hobbies occupy the hands of participants who might often be on their phones otherwise — have also made them appealing.

Here are six crafting retreats for all skill levels. Offered at multiple times, often in many locations, they tend to sell out fast. The attendance cost may not include lodging — be prepared to book that separately.

Working as a Broadway stage manager, Patty Lyons used to knit in her downtime. Now for seven years, she’s run a retreat at a Cooperstown, N.Y., hotel, attracting about 135 attendees each time. A wraparound porch overlooks a lake, and practically “every rocking chair has a knitter in it,” she said. Retreats are also held in Europe and Australia.

Activities have included a sheep documentary and a speaker from the Baseball Hall of Fame on vintage cardigans. Ms. Odom Stern even got up close with sheep in Scotland. Their warm wool has a special fuzz to it, she said.

Pricing for Cooperstown (on a wait list) varies from $995 to $1,255, including meals. A group rate for the hotel is offered separately. Pricing for an international retreat, including meals and lodging, varies depending on trip length, starting at $5,550.

For those with projects in quilting, or anything with yarn or wool, Sauder Village offers three-day retreats in a country inn in Archbold, Ohio. Guests can also indulge in horse-drawn carriage rides and roast s’mores.

That balance has kept Rita Thomas, a 72-year-old retired nurse from Port Clinton, Ohio, returning. She spends days on her rug-hooking projects and nights with friends at restaurants. Seeing old friends “is like a beautiful reunion of souls,” she said.

Pricing varies from $150 to $180, including some or all meals, but not lodging.

Start the day by exploring Fogo Island’s rugged coastline in Newfoundland, Canada. Then spend five hours immersed in pottery instruction.

That’s the rhythm of Fogo Clay Studio’s weeklong retreats, from April through October. Groups of eight stay in an ocean-view residence.

With the studio open 24 hours daily, guests can create several pieces, the studio owner, Sarah Fulford, said. Erna Snelgrove-Clarke, a 62-year-old professor based in Kingston, Ontario, described the community, food and pottery as “something special for your soul.”

Pricing, including meals and lodging, runs about $4,700.

Retreats from Thread Caravan, hosted all over the world for eight to 12 people over five to 10 days, begin with meeting local artisans, said Johanna Palmieri, the operations manager.

Recently in Oaxaca, Mexico, guests visited a top weaver’s textile studio and an archaeological site to see a motif used in rug designs. Barbara Gage, a 76-year-old retired teacher from Huntersville, N.C., has attended weaving and block-printing retreats, saying she has valued learning about different cultures and appreciated not handling logistics.

Pricing, including meals and lodging, varies by location. In Scotland, it can cost $7,600.

A needlepoint shop in a cabin in the foothills of the Blue Ridge Mountains? That’s where Stitching Fox offers three- and four-day retreats in Landrum, S.C., for guests stitching with silk-blended threads over hand-painted canvas. Daily classes capped at 14 run six hours. Guests can select a retreat where everyone works on one piece with the same canvas and threads, or one where they have their own canvases.

Dru Simpson, a 67-year-old tutor in college athletics from Winston Salem, N.C., has attended eight retreats, drawn to the atmosphere where women of all generations stitch together. To Ms. Simpson, needlepoint is both a calming therapy and an obsession.

A three-day retreat is $495 and a four-day one is $660, which includes catered lunch, but not lodging.

The American Quilters Society runs a five-day retreat at the National Quilt Museum in Paducah, Ky., and longer ones on cruise ships. In Kentucky, classes of 20 also explore nearby attractions. Cruise attendance is capped at 80 for classes and workshops. “You build your quilting network with new friends,” said Michelle Renee Hiatt, the society’s executive director.

That’s true for Deb Bondi, a 76-year-old retired human resources director from Prescott Valley, Ariz., who took a 16-day cruise to Hawaii in January after her husband died. She learned new techniques and bonded with friends; she and five women have since booked another cruise, to Panama.

Pricing for cruises vary, but can cost about $2,000 a week, including meals. The next Kentucky retreat will be announced in January; pricing typically runs $1,895, including lodging and most meals. A $30 annual society membership is required.

item.title: A U.N. Leader Focuses on the Deadly Problem of Road Safety
item.description:
During more than 20 years at the United Nations, Nneka Henry worked on big issues like poverty reduction, food security and women’s economic empowerment. In 2021 she took on another alarming and lingering global crisis — one that has been called the neglected pandemic — by becoming head of the U.N. Road Safety Fund.

The mix of cars, scooters, motorcycles and bicycles sharing the roads in the poorest nations has had a deadly impact. According to the World Health Organization, nearly 1.2 million lives — some 3,000 a day — are lost to vehicle crashes every year, with up to another 50 million serious injuries that often result in lifelong disabilities.

For children and young adults between 5 and 29, traffic injuries are the leading cause of death, the W.H.O. says.

“The risk of dying in a road crash is three times higher in low-income countries” than in high-income countries, said Ms. Henry. Poorly maintained roads and vehicles, lack of critical infrastructure like bike lanes and signage, and weak regulation and enforcement plague many countries; only a handful have comprehensive laws for drinking and driving; speeding; and seatbelt, child restraint and motorcycle use.

Ms. Henry focuses on strengthening systems for safe and sustainable transport. She was interviewed by phone at her home in Geneva, where the U.N. Road Safety Fund is based. The conversation has been edited and condensed.

What is the U.N. Road Safety Fund’s goal?

It’s a global partnership to protect and save lives. Road safety is a topic that is so unwieldy, so complex, that you really need a pooling of resources to effectively tackle it long term. It goes to the heart of the U.N. system, this vision that countries are working together to address problems that no country on its own can solve.

How does it work?

U.N. agencies, member countries, nongovernmental organizations, the private sector and other partners come together to help low- and middle-income countries, where 92 percent of the world’s road fatalities occur.

We’re on the ground trying to change policies, laws, how enforcement works, how data is collected, and how post-crash care treatment is applied. It’s about identifying what’s needed and transferring knowledge, expertise and financing to the people in the places that need it the most.

Why is the fund needed?

Crashes aren’t an inevitable cost of living in today’s world. Many are preventable. Countries that have halved or substantially reduced deaths have done so through action over many years and decades. Small, critical actions sustained over time can create lasting change. We just have to continue pushing through, building partnerships, doing the work that we know we need to do.

What is the scope of the work?

Projects range from creating safe school zones for children to increasing access to basic emergency care. Many revolve around strengthening regulations, like the Safer and Cleaner Used Vehicles Program. It improved safety and transport emissions standards on the importation of used vehicles to African countries and subsequently to nations in Asia, Latin America and the Caribbean.

Rwanda established a mandatory motorcycle helmet law and set up Africa’s first helmet testing lab. We set the standard and did the training, but the physical infrastructure was paid for by the FIA Foundation [which funds projects related to motor vehicles]. The lab is an example of how a growing number of countries are taking their results forward, investing their national budgets to continue the work beyond what we could have done.

In Armenia, sharing real-time road crash data and improving in-country coordination led to infrastructure upgrades — a new sidewalk, pedestrian crossing and traffic lights — on a high-risk road connecting two communities along an interstate highway. They’re already tracking fewer crashes and deaths from that intervention.

What persuades donors that a project is worth funding?

Evidence. Whenever I can get it, I use it because that’s what convinces and compels. And just being persistent, because it’s not easy going back to a donor multiple times over the course of years to make the case.

We’ve known that there has been an increase in motorcyclists’ deaths, but when the latest World Health Organization’s global status report on road safety came out, it was a wake-up call. I had donors who for years were saying they wouldn’t come on board. Now they’re putting millions down on the table and we have a growing portfolio of projects around motorcycle safety.

What’s been a notable challenge?

I didn’t expect that fund-raising would be such a big part of the role. There is no core funding at the U.N. for road safety, so funds for all the work that we do have to be voluntarily raised.

What motivates you?

Passion and results. I like to see change, like when a government is strengthening the law, adopting a new standard, or carving out some of its budget for road safety.

Do you have any role models?

One person who has particularly influenced me is my former boss at the International Trade Centre, Arancha González Laya. She was always prepared, always thinking things through. What difference can I make? If you’re going to the conference, it can’t just be to sit around. Who are you going to meet with? What are you trying to achieve? She was always strategizing, always thinking about how you can add value. These key leadership guidelines that she lived by were really inspiring.

item.title: Stocks Set to Slide as Tech Stocks Partly Reverse Nvidia-Sparked Rally
item.description:
Stock markets in the United States were set to slip on Tuesday, as premarket trading in technology shares tied to the artificial intelligence industry erased some of the heady rally the day before.

Investors have been buffeted by wrenching volatility in recent sessions, as tech stocks in particular have veered up and down, recording both their biggest daily rise and fall in more than a year in recent sessions. This pattern was set to extend into another day, with futures for major indexes turning lower ahead of the open of official trading in New York.

The S&P 500 was set to open nearly 1 percent lower. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite was set for a bigger decline, dragged down by Nvidia and other tech stocks. Both moves would only partially reverse the big gains at the start of the week.

Nvidia, which rocketed more than 30 percent on Monday after the reinstatement of the chip maker’s former chief executive, Jensen Huang, fell about 5 percent in premarket trading. Anthropic, the A.I. giant that broke records in its initial public offering last week, tumbled 6 percent, a move that would erase all of its gains since its market debut if it persisted through the day.

The hangover from Monday’s euphoric rally left many analysts wondering what to make of the return of Mr. Huang at Nvidia, which followed an extraordinary intervention by President Trump and even though the company’s board of directors had declared that the company founder would not be returning. Less than two weeks ago, Mr. Huang had resigned after revelations of an affair with a woman U.S. officials believe was spying for China and another with a subordinate.

“The on-again-off-again response from the board is, frankly, clown-like,” analysts at Bernstein wrote in a report. The recent turn of events “brings up legitimate questions as to their judgment and process which has to make one wonder how they come to their other important decisions,” they added. Mr. Huang’s record of keeping “questionable company on occasion” was also troubling for the market watchers who, nonetheless, were “happy to have Jensen back.”

The political intrigue behind Mr. Huang’s swift fall and sudden return weighed on analysts from Raymond James, who were unsure how the “internal struggle between national security hawks and more business-friendly factions” will play out within the Trump administration. “Recent developments suggest the political winds may be shifting, with commercial interests regaining influence, but the underlying tensions are far from resolved,” they wrote.

The slide in Anthropic’s high-profile shares also suggests wariness about the prospects for companies at the forefront of the A.I. boom. Fears about the sustainability of the rapid build-out of data centers and related infrastructure were already weighing on tech stocks before the turmoil at Nvidia.

“That financial markets moved on the employment prospects of one individual suggests either equity valuation models or current pricing might need to examined,” noted Paul Donovan, the chief economist at UBS Global Wealth Management.

The Nasdaq remains more than 10 percent below its peak in early October. Nvidia’s shares, even after Monday’s rally, which added roughly $1 trillion to its market value, are still down for the year.

item.title: Nvidia Intervention Heralds a New Kind of ‘Trumpian Socialism’
item.description:
As great-power politics increasingly revolve around technology, trade and finance, private businesses have been thrust to the front lines of foreign policy, often unwillingly.

For many global titans and mom-and-pop shops, the growing use of tariffs and export restrictions has forced them to sacrifice their bottom lines in the interests of national security.

Then there’s what happened this week.

President Trump’s decision to personally lobby Nvidia to rehire Jensen Huang as chief executive despite a China-related spy scandal reversed those priorities. Mr. Trump swept aside national security concerns to revive the fortunes of a single corporation — even a single executive — that he views as critical to the American economy and stock market.

“An individual C.E.O. has just demonstrated that the interests of his company can trump U.S. national security,” said Edward Fishman, director of the geoeconomics center at the Council on Foreign Relations.

Nvidia, a Silicon Valley giant worth some $4 trillion, has been at the center of an intense global competition with China for an edge in artificial intelligence. Mr. Huang resigned earlier this month after revelations that he had a relationship with a woman who U.S. intelligence officials believed was spying for the Chinese government.

Mr. Trump said he did not view Mr. Huang as a national security threat. “I just thought he should be running the company,” he told The New York Times on Monday.

His extraordinary intervention has surprised and worried Republican lawmakers in Washington and longstanding allies.

“It shocked me, to be honest,” Johann Wadephul, Germany’s foreign minister, said on Tuesday. “⁠In ⁠free, democratic and rules-based countries, political power should refrain from interfering ⁠in the economic engagement ​of companies.”

Presidents before have pushed into the affairs of industry and even individual companies during national emergencies and wartime.

But Julian E. Zelizer, a presidential historian at Princeton University, said Mr. Trump’s intervention is “very different from how other presidents have acted.”

“It’s the stock market first,” Mr. Zelizer said. “National security seems secondary. ”

President Harry S. Truman temporarily seized control of steels mills to prevent a strike during the Korean War. After the steel companies sued, the U.S. Supreme Court struck down the president’s order as unconstitutional.

A decade later, John F. Kennedy pressured steel companies to roll back a planned price increase. And in 2009, amid a quickening global financial crisis, Barack Obama pushed out the chairman of General Motors as part of a multibillion-dollar bailout of the auto industry.

But Mr. Trump’s role in the boardroom decisions of Nvidia is in a different category, historians and analysts said.

“This is a whole other level,” Mr. Zelizer said. “It’s a kind of Trumpian socialism we’re seeing.”

Mr. Trump’s move doubles down on other actions he has taken in the affairs of private companies. By the end of 2025, the Trump administration had committed more than $10 billion of taxpayer money to buy up ownership shares of companies it considered essential to national security, including Intel, Westinghouse and U.S. Steel.

Mr. Trump has cultivated relationships with technology chiefs, especially Mr. Jensen. In 2025, Nvidia agreed to give the federal government a cut of the revenue it generated from the sale of approved chips to China. It also said it would route deliveries of chips produced in Taiwan through the United States so the government could collect a 25 percent tariff and do security checks.

The administration’s dealings with Nvidia reflect a broader trend: the growing centrality of economic warfare.

Military conflicts, of course, continue. And nuclear weapons constitute a profound threat. But the world’s most powerful nations are relying more on their economic arsenals than their military ones.

The cooperative global order that prevailed after the fall of the Berlin Wall has crumbled, and statecraft has increasingly revolved around the tools of economic coercion. A long list of weapons have been put to greater use: tariffs, sanctions, export controls, the freezing of assets, prohibitions on financial transactions, access to loans and more.

The shift has at times pressed companies into active duty. President Joseph R. Biden Jr. barred Russia from the global financial system after it invaded Ukraine in 2022, counting on private banks rather than public offices to implement the restrictions.

Now the sweep of policy coming out of Washington is directly affecting the bottom line of companies and banks more than it has in the previous three decades, said Josh Lipsky, senior director of the GeoEconomics Center of the Atlantic Council, a research institute.

“I think that trajectory is only going to continue,” Mr. Lipsky said.

Government restrictions on international business dealings have soared, according to a recent study that surveyed earnings calls and analyst reports from thousands of firms around the world.

China has increasingly been a target. In 2022, the Biden administration imposed sweeping limits on China’s access to semiconductor and other technology. And last week, the Trump administration pushed ahead with a new rule to restrict China’s access to advanced A.I. chips through the use of data centers outside its borders.

China, too, has sharply stepped up its use of restrictions on exports. In 2023 and 2024, China designated five Western companies as “unreliable entities” and put them on its export control list. In 2025, 76 companies, including Raytheon, Boeing and Lockheed Martin, were added.

This spring, Beijing blocked Meta’s acquisition of an A.I. start-up founded by Chinese entrepreneurs, citing rules about foreign investment and technology exports. It has also kept a tight rein on the foreign sales of critical rare earth elements, using control over their export to punish and pressure trading partners on diplomatic issues like Taiwan.

“The share of global firms that report being affected by export controls has tripled in recent years compared to the 2010s,” said Matteo Maggiori, a professor of finance at Stanford Graduate School of Business, part of the team that conducted the research.

The vast majority of cases in which political leaders have sought to pressure countries abroad, Mr. Maggiori said, involved “private sector firms that are arm’s length from the government.”

American and European companies have frequently pushed backed against trade and other restrictions imposed by their democratically elected governments that they viewed as harmful.

By contrast, authoritarian governments in China and Russia have much tighter control of the market and businesses. That grip can be an advantage when a government wants to deploy economic tools to achieve foreign policy goals, Mr. Fishman at the Council on Foreign Relations noted.

When China imposes export controls, “it’s almost more like military power,” he said. “I do think there’s a real question around whether our distinctly American model of free market capitalism is well suited to the current age of geoeconomics.”

At the same time, he added, that model has produced extraordinary innovation, which has given the United States a strategic edge.

Mr. Trump’s intervention goes against that tradition. Mr. Wadephul, the German foreign minister, cited the Nvidia news in his speech before the Berlin Foreign Policy Forum on Tuesday. He warned against political leaders meddling so intimately in the affairs of private companies in democratic countries.

“I do have some doubts whether this is a very good model ⁠for the future,” he said.

Tatiana Firsova contributed reporting from Berlin.

item.title: National Security vs. the Stock Market
item.description:
Imagine it’s the Cold War. The head of a U.S. defense contractor has an affair with someone who the government determines is a Soviet asset. The affair is revealed, the chief executive resigns — then two weeks later the president himself pressures the company to rehire him.

Unthinkable? That’s kind of what just happened with Jensen Huang, the chief executive of the chip maker Nvidia, who recently resigned after admitting to an affair with a woman the U.S. government believes was a Chinese intelligence asset. President Trump not only pressured the company’s board into rehiring Huang. He also signaled that his Justice Department would not pursue any charges against him even as an investigation into chip smuggling to China is ongoing.

It’s an extraordinary degree of interference in a private company. Today my colleague Patti Cohen, our international economics correspondent, writes about how, under the Trump administration, national security seems to have taken a back seat to the stock market.

By Patricia Cohen

The increasing importance of technology, trade and finance to great-power politics means that in recent years, private businesses have, often unwillingly, been thrust to the front lines of foreign policy. Tools like tariffs and export restrictions mean global titans and mom-and-pop shops alike have had to sacrifice their bottom lines in the interests of national security.

Then there’s what happened this week.

President Trump’s decision to personally lobby Nvidia to rehire Jensen Huang as chief executive despite his involvement in a China-related spying scandal effectively reversed those priorities. (Yesterday, Huang told Nvidia employees that the notion that he is back because of Trump’s pressure on the company was “completely untrue.”)

Nvidia is a Silicon Valley giant worth some $4 trillion, and Huang is considered a singular figure in artificial intelligence. His resignation dragged down stock indexes, and prompted worries about the future of an industry that has been responsible for much of the stock market’s gains and the American economy’s growth.

Nvidia is also at the center of an intense global competition with China for an edge in A.I. Huang resigned after revelations of a relationship with a woman who U.S. intelligence officials believe was a Chinese asset, and whose company they believe was involved in helping China gain access to restricted A.I. chips.

And so Trump’s personal lobbying caused shock waves not only because of the level of presidential intervention in a private company’s affairs, but also the reasons he exercised such power.

“It’s the stock market first,” Julian E. Zelizer, a presidential historian at Princeton University, said. “National security seems secondary.”

An age of economic warfare

The Jensen Huang affair has come about at a moment when economic warfare is growing in importance. Increasingly, the world’s most powerful nations are relying on their economic arsenals in addition to their military ones. The long list of weapons includes tariffs, sanctions, export controls and more. And private companies have had to adapt.

Government restrictions on international business dealings have soared in recent years, according to a new study. One analyst told me that Washington policy is affecting the bottom lines of companies more now than it has in the previous three decades.

And few companies have been as central to the current superpower rivalry as Nvidia. In 2022, the Biden administration imposed sweeping limitations on China’s access to semiconductors and other computing technology. One product on the restricted list: the high-end models of Nvidia chips, considered the most advanced in the world. They have given the U.S. a crucial advantage in the fierce race between the U.S. and China to develop the most powerful A.I.

China, for its part, has fought back, designating companies, including defense giants like Raytheon, Boeing and Lockheed Martin as “unreliable entities” and putting them on its own export control list.

This spring, Beijing blocked Meta’s acquisition of an A.I. start-up founded by Chinese entrepreneurs, citing rules about foreign investment and technology exports. And of course, it has used its control over critical rare-earth elements to punish and pressure trading partners.

It’s in this environment that Trump has opted to sweep aside national security concerns in the service of a single corporation — and a single executive — whose fortunes he views as critical to the American economy and stock market.

When presidents lean on companies

Presidents have inserted themselves into the affairs of industry and even individual companies before. But what Trump did this week was “very different,” Zelizer said.

Harry Truman temporarily seized control of steel mills to prevent a strike during the Korean War. (After the steel companies sued, the U.S. Supreme Court struck down the president’s order as unconstitutional.)

A decade later, John F. Kennedy pressured steel companies to roll back a planned price increase. And in 2009, amid a spiraling global financial crisis, Barack Obama pushed out the chairman of General Motors as part of a multibillion-dollar bailout of the auto industry.

What’s made Trump’s interference so singular is that it took place even when there is no war or national emergency.

Trump has frequently pressured industry and company leaders. In his first term, he leaned on companies to not move production to Mexico. In his second, he went a step further and committed more than $10 billion of taxpayer money to buy up ownership shares of companies the administration considers essential to national security, including Intel, Westinghouse and U.S. Steel.

That unusual government intervention into the private market aroused concerns about conflicts of interest, market distortions and taxpayer losses. Now, Trump’s lobbying of Nvidia has set off new alarms.

“⁠In ⁠free, democratic and rules-based countries, political power should refrain from interfering ⁠in the economic engagement ​of companies,” Germany’s foreign minister, Johann Wadephul, said yesterday.

In an age of economic warfare, political leaders across the West have often made exceptions in the name of national security. What few have done, before this episode, is brush aside national security concerns to boost the prospects of a single C.E.O. and a stock market whose fortunes are so closely tied to his fate.

The latest:

Jensen Huang apologized to Nvidia employees and said he was in therapy.

Alice Huang, the woman at the center of the Nvidia spying scandal, grew up in a small factory town in China. Her jump to the tech world paralleled China’s own.

Ben Casselman, our chief economics correspondent, explains in the video below how the future of the U.S. economy is tied to A.I.

The Communist Party leader of Shanghai was placed under investigation as China’s leader, Xi Jinping, expanded his purge of party ranks.

A strike by Yemen’s Houthi militia on a skyscraper in Riyadh, the capital of Saudi Arabia, injured 11 people.

A French appeals court ruled that a police officer accused of fatally shooting a teenage driver will stand trial for murder.

The International Criminal Court got a boost from Japan, which welcomed the court’s president to Tokyo and pledged financial support.

Twenty-eight people remain unaccounted for after a fire at a candy factory in Indonesia that killed 26 people.

A U.S. jury found Huawei, the Chinese telecommunications giant, guilty of stealing trade secrets and evading sanctions against Iran.

An Iranian woman received 74 lashes for singing publicly in 2024 without a hijab.

Iraq’s prime minister ordered federal forces to take over border crossings and oil fields in the Kurdistan region.

A new book of excerpts from Pope Francis’ diary highlights his fears and doubts.

Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka, South Africa’s first female deputy president, died at 71.

As a new Miss Universe is set to be crowned, the organization has split into rival camps, and it’s hard to figure out who is actually in control.

The most clicked link in your newsletter yesterday was about travel with older adults.

Football: Senegal was ​reinstated as the winner of the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations ​after a successful court appeal.

Every fall, my Book Review colleagues put together a list of their favorite 100 fiction and nonfiction titles of the year. And every fall, I briefly feel very — inadequate!

This year’s list includes some of my own favorites (“London Falling” by Patrick Radden Keefe is the best thing I’ve read this year) and many more that I’ve never heard of. What I love most about the list is that you can use it to build a reading list based on other books you liked. I just finished “Tom Lake” by Ann Patchett and loved it. Apparently, that means I will probably like Barbara Kingsolver’s “Partita.” Sold. I shall report back!

Six years after they left Britain and their royal duties, Prince Harry and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, are back and settling into life as “private citizens.” They have a carefully managed program of public appearances that look distinctly royal at times, including bows and curtsies.

Buckingham Palace may have stripped away Harry and Meghan’s official status, but it has not stripped away their star power. Read more about their life as “nonroyal royals.”

American mahjong, the homegrown spinoff of the traditional Chinese game, has seemingly taken over the United States and ballooned into a multimillion-dollar industry. It comes with its own rules and modified tiles that render it nearly unrecognizable to devotees of the original game.

Critics have accused a few entrepreneurs of profiting from American mahjong while disrespecting the game’s cultural heritage. Read more about the mahjong turf war.

Discover: Agatha Christie’s West End thriller “The Mousetrap” begins its 75th year with a slick new staging.

Ask: A reader’s partner uses A.I. to write her love letters. Is she wrong to be upset?

Listen: Lana Del Rey and Dua Lipa added tracks to the Grand Theft Auto VI video game.

Laugh: Defuse awkward moments with humor. Here’s how.

A Spanish potato tortilla is an egg dish unlike any other. It doesn’t resemble the French omelet, which is loose and wobbly, or the Italian frittata, which is puffy and custardy. Instead, a tortilla is a solid cake, often enjoyed as a tapa.

Which river is this?

Beni River, Bolivia

Sepik River, Papua New Guinea

Peace River, Canada

Yangtze River, China

item.title: ‘Saturday Night Live’ Is Coming to France
item.description:
En direct de Paris, c’est Samedi soir!

A French version of “Saturday Night Live” is set to premiere next month, the premium television channel Canal+ announced on Tuesday.

Ten comedians who have worked in stand-up, film, theater and social media will form the show’s cast. The comedian and actor Manu Payet will host the premiere on Dec. 19.

A separate “S.NL.” offshoot that is now in its second season, “Saturday Night Live U.K.,” has hit its stride by leaning into its Britishness, skewering the Royal Family, “The Traitors” and former Prime Minister Keir Starmer.

Like the American and British versions of the show, the French edition is set to feature live sketches, recorded segments, musical guests and “a healthy dose of satire,” according to a statement from Canal+.

The cast members include Lison Daniel, who will also be on the writing staff and co-wrote “Call My Agent! The Movie”; Sawsan Abès, who is in the upcoming fourth season of “The White Lotus”; and Bérangère McNeese, a Belgian-American actress who spent part of her childhood in Kentucky.

The other cast members are Adel Fugazi, Emma Ebouaney, Simon Costi, Victor Sansano, Luca Besse, Bertrand Goncalves and François de Brauer.

The flagship American edition of “Saturday Night Live” celebrated its 50th anniversary last year. In its statement, Canal+ credited the original show’s longevity to an “almost audacious ability to reinvent itself, constantly keeping a finger on the pulse of an American society whose absurdities provide a nearly inexhaustible supply of fuel.”

It will not be the first time that France has tried out “Saturday Night Live.” In 2017, the comedian Gad Elmaleh hosted a one-off episode of a French version of the show, with a recreation of the famous “More Cowbell” sketch.

It was unclear when the second episode of the new adaptation would be broadcast. It will build on an overseas expansion for “Saturday Night Live.”

The British version of the show premiered in March on the channel Sky One with an initial run of eight episodes. It was renewed in May and returned in September, with more episodes planned, after a break, in January.

Many expected the show to fail, in part because of a history of comedy programs not always translating well when they cross the Atlantic and cynicism in the British news media.

But critics have said the show has found a fresh voice. Or as The Guardian wrote in May, “Predictions that ‘S.N.L. U.K.’ would be a national embarrassment have been categorically rubbished.”

In October, the British adaptation even took aim at the mother ship.

The comedian Shane Gillis generated controversy when he hosted the Oct. 10 episode in New York, calling women “whores” in his opening monologue for wearing shorts to the gym and using an expletive during a sketch. A week later, “Saturday Night Live U.K.” covered Gillis’s remarks in its “Weekend Update” segment, making a joke about Gillis and calling him a pair of expletives.

item.title: Diary of a Pope: New Book Offers Excerpts From Francis’ Journal
item.description:
In the waning weeks of 1992, a recently appointed auxiliary bishop in Buenos Aires named Jorge Mario Bergoglio took out a yearly planner bound with a black leather cover and began writing a diary. Three decades later, he was still at it — only now the diarist was known to the world as Pope Francis.

He wasn’t a constant chronicler of his life. Francis wrote on 86 pages before he became pope in 2013 and on only 55 more after he became leader of the Roman Catholic Church. Still, he appeared to understand the value of even the relatively modest material.

“From this, you will all see,” the pope declared when he showed the diary to Cardinal Victor Manuel Fernández, his top doctrinal watchdog, the cardinal recounts.

Cardinal Fernández, who was and remains one of Francis’ principal cheerleaders, appears to have taken that as a sign that the pope wanted his personal musings to become public. On Tuesday, he released a book drawing on them that he titled “The Private Diary of Pope Francis.”

Anyone hoping that the diary entries might offer insights into controversial papal decisions or even just dish a little gossip about Francis’ vast entourage of cardinals and cohorts may be disappointed. “The most confidential matters are written in code, using symbols that we cannot and should not decipher,” Cardinal Fernández writes.

The cardinal also redacted the entries, eschewing chronology and, in many cases, context.

But with Cardinal Fernández as a guide, readers can nevertheless have a glimpse into some of Francis’ most intimate fears and struggles, as well as a better understanding of the traits that helped forge his public persona.

Here are some of the highlights.

Francis said that he often struggled with moments of human weakness and that it caused him pain.

“The Lord allowed me to see the greatness of my baseness,” he wrote on April 18, 2010. “I saw how many times I allow feelings of disdain, envy, pride to overtake me. I feel so ashamed.”

On Dec. 30, 2022, he bemoaned “the proud, self-sufficient, cynical, self-deceptive Jorge,” and on other occasions said he felt inadequate about his ministry.

In the book, Cardinal Fernández casts the pope’s self-awareness of his own failings as courageous. Francis’ “heartfelt self-accusation,” he writes, had a “healing, peaceful and liberating effect on his heart, which at the same time, prevented judging others.”

Francis was driven by a sense of mission and a discipline born of his early training.

“Strong movement not to protect myself behind a schedule but instead to be available for whatever is asked of me,” he wrote when he was still an archbishop on Dec. 4, 1994. “Not to defend what I like and my time.”

As pope, he kept a grueling schedule, despite health issues that eventually caught up with him.

Francis was already 76 when elected and determined to make the most of the papacy because he suspected he would not hold the position for long. That belief crops up often in the diary.

The entries suggest that he was not afraid of death, but he did grow upset over the years when people treated him as elderly. Of one encounter, he wrote on July 31, 2011: “He told me three times that I’m an old man. He’s the first person who dared say this to me. I must bear it.”

There are several references to the devil in the diary, as well as to visions of Hell.

In the last entry, written on Aug. 18, 2024, eight months before his death, Francis wrote:

“In briefly running through my life, I saw moments in which the devil made himself present …I felt the Lord’s invitation to be more attentive and more careful and not to assent to [the devil’s] presence. I beg the Virgin to protect and help me.”

These musings fit with Francis’ messaging throughout his papacy, as he often spoke about Satan’s malevolent presence in the world.

In 2015, he said the devil was punishing Mexico with violence.

In a 2018 apostolic exhortation, “Rejoice and Be Glad,” he noted that in biblical times, “epilepsy, for example, could easily be confused with demonic possession,” but added a caution. The faithful, he said, should not conclude “that all the cases related in the Gospel had to do with psychological disorders and hence that the devil does not exist or is not at work.”

And speaking on prime-time television in 2021, Francis said there was something “almost satanic” about the high number of cases of women who had been victims of domestic violence.

In 2021 and 2022, Francis experienced a crisis that, he wrote on Dec. 30, 2022, took the form of “withdrawal and worldliness.” He referred to it as being “mixed with governance issues, pressure regarding decisions to make, and aridity and desolation.”

It is here that some readers may find the scarcity of context especially frustrating. But in the end, while the diary entries were written by Francis, the book itself is the work of Cardinal Fernández — and he makes clear he is willing to go only so far.

At its outset, he says he does not “intend to elaborate my own theories about Pope Francis in this book or to offer a personal study or interpretation regarding his thought.”

Still, Cardinal Fernández relents a bit in presenting the excerpts about the crisis. It involved, he says, temptation related to the use of power and regrets about the “lack of goodness in his motivations and aspirations.”

item.title: Harry and Meghan Are ‘Private Citizens.’ Some in Britain Curtsy Anyway.
item.description:
When Prince Harry and Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, visited a food bank last month in Nottingham, England, they had a request. No formal etiquette. No need for the bows or curtsies that are traditional for members of the royal family. They could be greeted simply as “Harry and Meghan.”

The co-founder of the charity, Sajid Mohammed, obliged with an ordinary handshake. But around him, people curtsied, some volunteers wept with emotion, and six parents tried to bring their babies forward.

Even royals who have stepped back from official duties still inspire reflexive ceremony in some parts of the British public, it turns out.

“It’s very much like Harry’s mother, the late Princess Diana,” Mr. Mohammed said in an interview afterward. “There’s an aura around the couple. It’s beyond normal celebrity.”

The rapturous response they received in Nottingham underlines the challenge, and potential benefit, that the newly repatriated Sussexes offer to Britain’s monarchy, six years after they left the country and their royal duties. Queen Elizabeth II reluctantly blessed their self-imposed exile in 2020 but said that they must give up state funding and could no longer be considered full working royals.

Their return to Britain, which Harry said in a recent GQ interview was to pursue “opportunities for the family” and to school their children, has resurfaced questions about their status. They appear intent on carving out a specific profile, managing public appearances on their own terms and tightly controlling what they share, including where in England they have chosen to live, a fact that remains undisclosed. Their careful image management partly reflects the couple’s fraught relationship with the British media and its often hostile coverage in the past, which they previously said had contributed to their departure from Britain.

For now, their popularity in opinion polls remains low, particularly compared with Harry’s older brother, Prince William, and his wife Catherine, Princess of Wales. But can a pair armed with Hollywood glamour and global celebrity operate on their own terms without eclipsing the traditional working royals they left behind? Could their return, if managed well, inject energy into the institution as King Charles III enters his twilight years?

Charles has attempted to hold the line his mother drew. After Harry and Meghan’s return to Britain in late August, a letter was sent on the king’s behalf to government officials, stiffly reminding them that the Sussexes were “private citizens” who must not be addressed as “His and Her Royal Highness.”

The difficulty for Buckingham Palace is that, while it could strip away their official status, it cannot strip away their star power.

On the day the Sussexes swept through Nottingham, the king was in Cardiff opening the Senedd, the Welsh Parliament. While the BBC covered both events, ITV’s evening bulletin only found room for Harry and Meghan. The following day, Peter Hunt, a former BBC royal correspondent, highlighted the newspaper front pages smothered in Sussex coverage, writing on social media: “The palace spin is failing on contact with reality. Harry and Meghan are royals. End of.”

The daily grind of the British crown is not, by design, thrilling. It’s built on unglamorous routine — bronze plaques unveiled at rain-swept civic centers and ribbon-cuttings at community clinics — the stoic pattern perfected by Princess Anne, Charles’s sister.

“One of the biggest risks of Harry and Meghan coming back is that they take attention away from the core work of the monarchy, which is slightly dull at times,” said Craig Prescott, a constitutional scholar and author.

That dynamic is particularly delicate around major overseas excursions, when palace orthodoxy holds that royals should not compete with royals on big tours. When Charles toured the Caribbean this month, the Sussexes avoided rival public appearances.

Other overlaps are harder to prevent. Prince Harry’s GQ interview was published as Charles and Queen Camilla welcomed the Sultan of Oman on a state visit to Windsor Castle. Critics immediately claimed Harry was upstaging a diplomatic event, but supporters noted that the interview had been taped a month earlier in New York and that its publication had been scheduled by the magazine.

The couple’s carefully curated schedule of activities since returning to England certainly resembles, at times, the diplomatic and charitable engagements that define royal life. In September, Harry attended London’s WellChild Awards, honoring seriously ill children. The couple appeared at the European Parliament in Brussels, where Harry spoke about digital safety and child protection. This month, Harry made a surprise visit to Ukraine, meeting wounded veterans preparing for his Invictus Games, and last week he made an unannounced appearance on ITV’s “This Morning,” where he joked that he was “squeezing” the American accents out of his kids and helped make a Christmas cake.

“You might describe them as nonroyal royals,” said Mr. Prescott.

For Epic Partners, a Nottingham charity that runs programs for disadvantaged young people, Harry and Meghan’s visit to the city in October helped “raise our profile,” said Pete Bewley, the charity’s chief executive. “People in the U.K. love the royals, and they are part of that, even if they’re not working royals officially.”

Off camera, the couple has settled into a quieter routine. While they have not disclosed where they are living and asked the media not to reveal their children’s schools, they have been spotted in pubs around the Cotswolds — an idyllic pocket of southern England beloved by wealthy Americans.

Their commercial interests complicate the picture. Meghan continues to build her lifestyle label, As Ever, and recently signed on as a guest judge for “Junior MasterChef Australia.”

Blending enterprise with royal ties has historically proved fraught. When Prince Michael of Kent, Queen Elizabeth II’s cousin, sat with Larry King on CNN in the 1990s to peddle merchandise tied to the House of Windsor — branded ties, china and glassware — biographers noted that Elizabeth was not amused. Years later, when the Sussexes proposed their own “half-in, half-out” arrangement at the Sandringham negotiations in 2020, she proved equally unimpressed.

Today, some wonder whether the couple have managed to carve out that settlement on their own. “It looks like they’ve got what they wanted six years ago, which is that half-in-half-out role,” Katie Nicholl, who writes about the royals, said recently on her podcast, “The Royals Uncensored.”

But their present arrangement is fundamentally different. They carry no official duties, hold no royal patronages. Whether that proves sustainable may depend on how the couple and the palace manage the attention. While Harry has reconciled with his father, his relationship with his brother William, the heir to the throne, appears to be as frosty as ever, with no reported interactions since the Sussexes returned.

Nor does a warm reception at a charity signal a broader recovery in public affection. A recent YouGov poll put Harry’s domestic approval at 29 percent and Meghan’s at 20 percent, with deep scars lingering over their noisy 2020 exit.

Ed Owens, a royal historian, noted that a “quiet rehabilitation” is never out of the question in Britain, pointing to Camilla’s decades-long journey from tabloid pariah to queen consort. Charles, too, has lived a life of many chapters — deeply unpopular during the breakdown of his marriage to Diana, he has since seen both his public standing recover and his environmental views become mainstream.

“As long as there isn’t deliberate, direct and obvious competition between the working royals and Harry and Meghan, both could stand to benefit from their association with each other,” Mr. Owens said.

item.title: Radio Offers Russian Troops Classic Rock, Nostalgia — and Pleas to Surrender
item.description:
On a highway in eastern Ukraine, the car radio started to crackle about 30 miles outside the city of Izium. Soon a classic Russian rock song came through clearly, followed by Russian punk, pop, ballads and a synth favorite.

The proximity of the front line and occupied territories has long meant that Russian stations could be picked up in the area. But listening more closely to this one revealed a different kind of D.J.

Tucked into a stream of Russian hits was a spoken-word track, “Instructions for Surrender.” This seemingly Russian radio station is actually a psychological operation aimed at subverting Russian soldiers’ morale.

As they battle on land, in the sky and on the sea, Ukraine’s special operations forces are also waging war on the airwaves. Undermining Russian soldiers’ “desire to fight,” said the D.J., “is the main goal.” In keeping with Ukrainian military protocols, he goes by the call-sign Humanist.

War is a young man’s game, a cure against wrinkles

— “Star Called Sun,” by Kino

Radio has been used as a weapon in conflicts for decades. Psychological operations, or PsyOps, even longer.

During World War II, “Tokyo Rose” and “Axis Sally” broadcast radio propaganda aimed at demoralizing U.S. troops. In Vietnam, “Hanoi Hannah” tried to convince American G.I.’s that the war was immoral, interspersing messages with antiwar songs from the likes of Pete Seeger, Joan Baez and Bob Dylan. The U.S. military had its own radio PsyOp, transmitting broadcasts into the northern provinces of South Vietnam.

In the war in Ukraine, similar efforts have come with a high-tech twist thanks to artificial intelligence that can help craft the songs.

When the Ukrainian project was getting off the ground in 2024, Russia was using a powerful transmitter in Belgorod to broadcast propaganda across the border into Ukraine’s Kharkiv region. A special forces serviceman, who helped deploy some of Ukraine’s first radio transmitters, said the military sought to jam the Russian frequency and replace it with its own broadcast.

The initial programming contained no music, only appeals for Russians to lay down their weapons, messages about the war’s futility and calls for civilians to evacuate frontline areas. Then the Ukrainians decided to add tunes hoping to hook frontline Russian soldiers who stumbled upon the frequency.

The Ukrainians initially relied heavily on A.I. to create new songs that exploited nostalgia for Soviet history, sounded Moscow-made and adjusted the lyrics of tracks.

These days, such productions are the minority. Most songs on Ukraine’s PysOps playlists in the Kharkiv region are unaltered Russian hits, since there is a wealth of ready-made material to choose from.

This train is on fire, and we have nowhere left to run

This land was ours until we got bogged down in the struggle

— “Train on Fire,” by Aquarium

Russian artists have long used song to question and critique the country’s wars, through Chechen bard ballads, Soviet-Afghan war rock and Perestroika-era punk. Many became anthems, now being used for what Ukraine hopes is its own benefit.

Ukraine’s special operations forces have a network of transmitters around the country running the PsyOp broadcasts.

Programming differs from sector to sector, making each transmitter akin to a local radio station. Musical blocks are broken up with news from that area of the front and about prisoners of war — through a Ukrainian lens — and instructions on how to surrender.

“First — find a white cloth and tie it to something that can be raised above your head, for example, to a stick. Yell loudly ‘I surrender.’ Put down your weapon and raise your hands above your head. Second — get out of the trench, tank, APC. Third — take off your body armor, helmet and lie on the ground, and wait for the Ukrainian military to approach you.”

In the Donetsk region, one station broadcasts as “Radio Station Choose Life.” Around Izium, where the station calls itself “Radio Infantry,” the voice behind the microphone is Humanist. He’s 34 and a hard man to track down.

After stumbling upon the signal in April, reporters from The New York Times returned to the area in May to record the station and figure out who was broadcasting. After a series of twists, turns and misdirections, Ukraine’s special operations forces acknowledged their role.

The Times was not permitted to visit the station itself and was only allowed to interview those involved over video calls. Humanist, the coordinator and content manager, appeared against a beige background completely covered except for his eyes, yanking up a black balaclava that kept slipping down.

He said he worked in an ordinary room with windows — no vinyl on the walls — alongside soldiers performing non-radio-related tasks. The operation is “simply a guy sitting at a laptop,” stitching audio tracks together, he said.

Growing up in central Ukraine, Humanist said, he once dreamed of becoming a scientist or an archaeologist. He later hoped to become a soldier — and that dream came true.

“You will freeze, see death and its evil grin

And in a quiet whisper, you sold your soul to the devil”

— “Extinguished Candle,” by Timur Mutsurayev

He said the broadcast experimented with different approaches, like retransmitting Ukrainian radio, but now uses only original playlists.

The vibe, Humanist said, is “drowsily nostalgic.”

The station tries to evoke homesickness and “a depressive mood,” he said, with a message “that nothing good awaits them, that war is always, first and foremost, blood, death, and fatalities, and that they are unlikely to see the end of this war, and that it would be much better to stop fighting.”

He relies on “opposition-oriented” Russian music genres, particularly antiwar songs, that could be “described as demotivating.”

“There are actually quite a lot of them,” he said. “They were created at different times, but each one is cool in its own way, each one touches the soul in its own way.”

Like songs by Viktor Tsoi, the star of the band Kino. He died in 1990, but his work helped establish rock as the soundtrack of the fall of Communism in Eastern Europe.

Or Boris Grebenshikov, the lead singer of Aquarium, who has been active since the 1970s. An outspoken critic of the war in Ukraine, he lives in exile in London.

And Timur Mutsurayev, the Chechen bard of the 1990s and 2000s whom Humanist recalled hearing played during his first military service in 2014.

Humanist said he doubted whether most Russians today appreciated the struggle imbued in the songs of an earlier generation, or if the songs packed the same emotional punch. Yet maybe subconsciously, he said, the messages resonate.

Take the early 1980s anthem “Don’t Shoot” by DDT, inspired by the Soviet-Afghan war. It is perfect for the playlist, Humanist said, because it has an antiwar message and “it is a good, high-quality song.”

Standing before him as if alive was that kid, the one who had begged him for just one thing:

Don’t shoot! Don’t shoot! Don’t shoot! Don’t shoot!

Aquarium’s overtly antiwar hit “Train on Fire,” from 1987, holds similar power, Humanist said, with a message “that we are going in the wrong direction.”

Humanist said his own musical taste tends toward patriotic Ukrainian songs, but it all depends on his mood. Lately that has meant listening to a lot of “Zhadan and the Dogs” — a ska punk band from the Kharkiv region.

He laughed when asked if any listener complaints have made it across his desk, maybe from Ukrainians confused by the broadcast.

“We’re not that easy to find in order to express dissatisfaction,” he said. But he admitted that he has turned on the station while driving and had passengers ask why Russian music is on the airwaves — to which he’s proudly replied it’s no accident.

Michael Schwirtz contributed reporting.

item.title: Norway Has Closed Its Last Coal Mine, Ending a Way of Life in the Arctic
item.description:
At the end of their final shift in Norway’s last coal mine, dust clinging to their overalls, the miners stopped work to listen to a solemn song.

The one who performed, in his hard hat, strummed a guitar as he sang, “We are a coal mining problem in a tourist town.”

It was a lament for a way of life at Mine 7, on Svalbard, an ice-covered, Norwegian-controlled archipelago not far from the North Pole. The mine was unprofitable and Norway’s state-owned mining company shut it down this spring, the last step in a long process of ending Norwegian coal mining.

Politicians are betting that the future of Svalbard — home to rugged glaciers, arctic foxes and views of the northern lights — does not belong to coal’s dirt and grime.

“Longyearbyen is founded on mining history and miners,” Gudmund Lovli, the lead miner, said at the closing ceremony, naming the town, Svalbard’s main settlement, that staffed Mine 7. “It’s removing a workplace that we’ve grown to love.”

As the ceremony finished, the miners wrapped a symbolic chain and padlock around the gate and threw the key down the shaft.

Norway asserted its right over Svalbard when mining brought global interest to what had been an icy wilderness. Longyearbyen, its biggest town, has been home to Norwegian mining families for more than a century. But in less than a generation, the town has changed. First, international researchers came to study the Arctic habitat. Now it is also a cruise ship destination, with expensive hotels, upscale restaurants and 150,000 tourists a year, dwarfing its population of about 2,500.

It is also an unlikely geopolitical hot spot. Norway is pushing to more firmly assert its control over Svalbard and fend off foreign influence in the Arctic. The islands have a unique position enshrined in a 1920 treaty, which says anyone can work there, on condition of recognizing Norway’s sovereignty. The only other state with a permanent settlement on Svalbard is Russia.

The miners feel trapped by changes beyond their control.

Things that used to be just everyday features of life — carrying a gun to ward off polar bears or finding a spot to leave your sled dog — have become novelties for tourists posing for selfies.

Against the Arctic wilderness, the miners’ brightly painted houses are a spot of color. In one kindergarten, named “Kullungen,” or “the Coal Kid,” all the classrooms were named after mines.

But, without work, most miners have left and found jobs in other industries.

Tools once used in Mine 7 are now on display at the Svalbard museum. At the Karlsberger pub, portraits of miners at work feel like pictures of a bygone era. The pub’s owner, Steve Daldorff Torgersen, who has lived on Svalbard for 36 years and weathered many changes, said the finality of Mine 7’s closing had been a shock.

“It feels sad and strange,” he said during a recent interview. “Mentally, it’s a catastrophe.”

Ingrid Fiskaa, a member of Parliament from the Socialist Left Party, visited Svalbard just before Mine 7 closed, and said she had come away worrying that the people of Longyearbyen would feel forgotten. The closure was emotional, but the mine wasn’t viable to keep open, she said, suggesting instead that Svalbard embrace other industries.

“I don’t think mining is the key here,” she said. “We need economic activity, business activity, because that’s a vital part of keeping a vibrant local community to enforce our sovereignty.”

The last day was a long time coming. In 2021, as Norway cast itself as a green power, the state-owned mining company, Store Norske, informed Parliament that it planned to close Mine 7. It had already closed a larger mine, sending hundreds of miners and their families to the mainland. But Russia’s war in Ukraine created a brief coal boom, which kept the last and smallest Norwegian mine open until now.

When the closure finally came this year, the mine became the center of a renewed political debate about how to ensure that Norway retained control of Svalbard.

When Norway first laid claim to the archipelago after World War I, it used coal mining and mineral exploration to strengthen its hold. With recent discoveries of rare earth minerals on the ocean floor nearby, critics of the closure say another country, like Russia, could use mineral exploration in its own claim.

Marius Arion Nilsen, a conservative Norwegian lawmaker who recalled crouching through Mine 7’s tight tunnels on a recent visit, lobbied Parliament to force the state mining company to keep it open. He also proposed that Norway should look into opening a new mine for minerals. He is convinced that closing Mine 7 is a political and economic mistake that will favor Russia and its allies.

“To continue on this route, on this path, with today’s world and today’s uncertainties, in terms of geopolitics and supply chains, it’s unfathomable,” he said.

Russia is still digging. Barentsburg, a mining town of 300, is a Russian outpost in the Arctic: The signs are Cyrillic, a wooden Orthodox chapel is one of the tallest buildings, and a bust of Lenin stares out.

Some Norwegian miners said they saw their jobs as part of an unofficial deterrence strategy.

“If there were to be a bigger political conflict now, they might realize that they have to open a new mine,” said Emil Aspen Stenslokken, who sent his family to the mainland while he took a job with Svalbard’s small fire department.

Jon Gunnar Hansen, the miner who wrote and performed the closing song, remained as part of a small crew stripping the mine. He still wears his overalls and hard hat to salvage rubber, electrical wiring and motors.

Close to retirement, Mr. Hansen has yet to figure out whether he’ll find a new job, how long he can stay in the apartment he rents from the mining company, and whether he’ll leave Svalbard for Norway, as he called it, before thinking again and referring to the mainland.

“If you’re a politician, and you want people to vote for you, opening coal mines isn’t the best thing these days,” he said. “At least, not in Norway.”

item.title: Shanghai’s Party Leader Is Put Under Investigation as Xi’s Purges Expand
item.description:
The Communist Party leader of Shanghai, Chen Jining, has been placed under investigation on suspicion of “serious violations,” the Chinese government announced on Tuesday. It was a stunning downfall for an official who had widely been seen as destined for a higher role under the country’s top leader, Xi Jinping.

The investigation into Mr. Chen was announced in a brief bulletin from Xinhua, China’s official news agency, which gave no details about reasons. The bulletin said that Mr. Chen was suspected of “serious violations of discipline and the law,” a phrase that usually refers to allegations of corruption.

Mr. Chen, 62, an environmental scientist trained in Britain, rose as a university president and minister for environmental protection. He went on to become mayor of Beijing and, from 2022, party secretary of Shanghai — a key post in charge of one of China’s most important commercial cities. Previous Shanghai party secretaries have often risen to a seat on the party’s Politburo Standing Committee, a core leadership body that currently has seven members, led by Mr. Xi.

Mr. Chen’s abrupt undoing suggests that Mr. Xi’s expanding drive against corruption and disloyalty means that even seemingly secure protégés cannot feel safe as he prepares to claim an all-but-certain fourth term ruling China. Other officials made subject to investigations have gone on to face prosecution, conviction and imprisonment.

“This is shocking,” Wang Hsin-hsien, a professor at National Chengchi University in Taiwan who studies the Chinese Communist Party, said of the announcement of an investigation into Mr. Chen.

“There might well be more major shake-ups to come,” he added. “If even Chen Jining has been taken down, the same could happen to others. There’s no safety for anyone.”

Later on Tuesday, the Shanghai Communist Party leadership announced that it had endorsed the removal of Mr. Chen and pledged loyalty to Mr. Xi at a meeting. There must “always be absolute loyalty to the party,” the official summary of the meeting said.

One month ago, Mr. Xi presided over a meeting of the Communist Party Central Committee where he called for a renewed campaign for discipline and loyalty. The meeting also announced preparations for a party congress next year, at which Mr. Xi is almost certain to win another five years as general secretary.

This month, Mr. Chen convened a meeting in Shanghai where he warned officials to abide by Mr. Xi’s warnings against corruption and other abuses of power. “Elevate your political stance, and remain clearheaded and vigilant,” Mr. Chen told them.

Last week, Mr. Xi was in the international limelight as he hosted President Trump and President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia for a brief three-way summit in the southern city of Shenzhen, and Mr. Xi may have waited until after that meeting before moving against Mr. Chen, Professor Wang said.

Mr. Xi could become increasingly preoccupied with cleaning out the party and the military ahead of the party congress, at which he will choose a new generation of leading officials, said Christopher K. Johnson, a former senior China analyst at the C.I.A.

“Chen’s downfall is a stark reminder that, despite all the fanfare over last week’s trilateral summit with Presidents Putin and Trump, and China’s ongoing competition with the United States, Xi remains laser-focused on the politics around his bid for a fourth term at next year’s party congress,” said Mr. Johnson, who is now head of the political risk firm China Strategies Group.

Since Mr. Xi began his third leadership term in 2022, investigations and removals have brought down around 100 senior military officers and a growing number of civilian party officials. In July, the party expelled Ma Xingrui, another senior official, after accusing him of corruption and of abusing his power for favors and sex.

“As with Xi’s purge of the high command, he is telegraphing he intends to cut deep into the party’s senior ranks to find officials he thinks he can trust,” Mr. Johnson said.

Many analysts thought that Mr. Chen could rise to become premier, or at least a vice premier, in Mr. Xi’s next administration. Mr. Chen had won a reputation as a technocrat whose scientific education blended well with Mr. Xi’s technological priorities.

Mr. Chen was also already a member of the party’s Politburo, a wider council of leading central and local officials. He is now virtually certain to be expelled from the party and from the Politburo, which would mean that four of the 24 Politburo members elected in 2022 had been removed and investigated. One of those was Zhang Youxia, China’s topmost general until his removal this year.

“While the specifics about Chen Jining are not yet clear, the effect will be that the other members of the Politburo will be living in dread,” Professor Wang said.
