item.title: Dozens Unaccounted for Days After Factory Fire in Indonesia
item.description:
The death toll at a candy factory in Indonesia consumed by a fire rose to 26 on Tuesday and was expected to worsen as rescue workers gingerly made their way to a stairwell on the second floor of the building.

“We suspect this area, which served as an exit route for employees, may contain many more bodies,” a rescue worker identified as Vicky said in a video shared with reporters by the Indonesian authorities.

Twenty-eight people remain unaccounted for after the fire, which broke out at a facility in Serang, Banten Province, about 50 kilometers, or 30 miles, from the capital, Jakarta

Wearing surgical gloves and a gas mask that dangled around his neck, Vicky explained in the video how rescue workers were carefully lifting layer after layer of steel. “The building’s structural integrity is failing,” he said. “Using our cutting tools could trigger vibrations, potentially causing a collapse that would put us at risk.”

The blaze at the factory, which is owned by the company Fonusa Agung Mulia and made milk candies and lollipops, started on Saturday afternoon and raged for several hours. The company said 300 people were inside the factory compound on that day, with 65 believed to be in the area where the fire broke out.

Firefighters cooled the charred debris and mangled steel beams well into Monday to prevent flames from reigniting.

“Many victims were found on the second floor,” Al Amrad, who leads the search and rescue agency in Banten Province, said in a phone interview, adding that he could not confirm whether those workers had been trying to reach an emergency exit.

The authorities said that of the 26 fatalities, nine were believed to be women and seven were believed to be men. The police said that the gender of the remaining 10 could not be determined yet because their bodies were too charred.

As of Monday, 31 relatives of missing workers had provided DNA samples. Three of those workers have been confirmed safe and returned home, the police said.

The police said on Tuesday that they had opened a criminal investigation.

“We have identified indications of a criminal offense involving negligence or carelessness that led to the fire,” said Zain Dwi Nugroho, the deputy chief of Banten’s regional police, although he did not elaborate on what evidence investigators had gathered so far.

Fonusa Agung Mulia’s chief executive, Steven Wijaya, said during a news conference on Sunday that the company regularly organized emergency drills, and apologized to the victims’ families.

After a visit to the site on Monday, Said Iqbal, an adviser to President Prabowo Subianto of Indonesia, said that the authorities were investigating whether a short circuit in the building’s air conditioning system had triggered the fire.

item.title: A Lion on the Loose Near Istanbul? Not So Fast.
item.description:
When officials in Istanbul said over the weekend that a lion had been spotted prowling a leafy suburb north of the city, Turkish authorities sprang into action.

They deployed drones and thermal cameras to scan the woodlands where surveillance cameras were said to have captured blurry footage of the animal near a sports facility. Veterinarians and wildlife experts placed baits and motion-sensor traps. Security forces fanned out as a forest in the area was sealed off and residents were warned to be careful, according to the state-run Anadolu news agency.

But late on Monday, after more than 24 hours of extensive searching and media frenzy, the authorities suddenly backtracked: There was no lion on the loose. The creature in the footage wasn’t a lion at all.

“After examining new footage from different angles, it is concluded that the animal was not a lion or any other kind of big cat,” the Istanbul governor’s office said in a statement.

Was it an oversized house cat? A dog in disguise? Another kind of wild creature?

That is now anyone’s guess. Overhead thermal camera footage released by the police and grainy CCTV clips published by Turkish media have done little to clarify the mystery animal’s identity.

While the search fueled anxiety and left some local residents flustered, some have since embraced A.I.-generated videos of a big cat playfully interacting with people in the streets of Istanbul.

The city, a sprawling metropolis of 15 million people and several forests, is known for the hospitality it extends to stray cats. In June, a cat interrupted a performance of the “Romeo and Juliet” ballet by Prokofiev.

It is not, however, a haven for lions.

Still, in the past, it was not unheard-of for some wealthy Turks to keep the African wildcats as rare pets. So when reports spread that a lion was roaming a forest, some assumed it had escaped a private residence nearby. Uskumrukoy, the neighborhood where the animal was first spotted on Sunday evening, is an affluent suburb of Istanbul.

“It was certainly an animal someone was looking after in his home,” Seyda Ust, an elected official in the neighborhood, said on Sunday evening as news of an escaped feline spread. While the authorities never specified the animal’s gender, many concluded it was a lioness because the footage suggested it did not have the mane typically seen on males.

In the early hours of Monday, the search ramped up. “The lion’s location has been identified,” the governor’s office said at the time, “and all necessary measures are being taken to capture it alive.” Wildlife experts and veterinarians took to television and social media to explain how to behave if one were to encounter the feline.

In a later statement, the governor’s office reiterated that it had acted on a tip and insisted that “prioritizing the safety of our citizens, we meticulously evaluate all reports.”

“Our teams are ready to reassess the situation should any new information become available,” it added.

item.title: 2 Men Arrested on Suspicion of Breaking Into Prince William and Catherine’s Country Home
item.description:
Two men have been arrested on suspicion of breaking into the country home of Prince William, the heir to the British throne, and his wife, Catherine, Princess of Wales.

The couple and their family were not at the property, Anmer Hall, near Sandringham in Norfolk at the time on Monday night but were at their main residence, Forest Lodge, at Windsor.

The intrusion will raise questions about the security of Britain’s royal residences.

In a statement, the Norfolk police said on Tuesday that two men had been arrested “on suspicion of burglary following an incident at a property on the Sandringham Estate,” adding that officers were called just before 6 p.m. after a report of suspicious activity at the address.

“Officers attended and specialist resources, including police dogs, drones and the National Police Air Service helicopter, were deployed to assist with searches in the area,” the statement said. “Two men were arrested on the estate on suspicion of burglary and trespass. They remain in police custody.”

Kensington Palace said that it would not comment on security matters.

Anmer Hall, which is thought to have 10 bedrooms and is on the Sandringham Estate of King Charles III, was a wedding present to William and Catherine from Queen Elizabeth II.

It was built in 1802, was purchased by the future Edward VII in 1896 and was described as a “delightful but minor Georgian manor house” by one leading British art historian, Roy Strong.

The property also has a swimming pool and a tennis court, according to British media reports.

News of the break-in came as William met Britain’s prime minister, Andy Burnham, in 10 Downing Street. The two men have met before, but this visit was the first by a senior member of the royal family to the prime minister’s official residence since Queen Elizabeth II was there in 2012.

item.title: Japan’s Leader, in Break with U.S., Defends International Criminal Court
item.description:
The International Criminal Court has faced a series of grave threats recently: severe sanctions from the Trump administration, acute budget strains and denunciations from China, Russia and the United States.

But on Tuesday the court got a boost from a critical ally, as Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi of Japan welcomed the court’s president, Judge Tomoko Akane, to Tokyo and vowed to accelerate financial support.

“The Japanese government will continue to provide robust support to the I.C.C.,” Ms. Takaichi wrote on X after the meeting, “ensuring that it can effectively fulfill its intended role and functions in upholding the ‘rule of law.’”

Ms. Takaichi’s comments were a rare break from President Trump, whose administration has led an aggressive effort recently to rein in the global body. Her appearance with Judge Akane, a renowned Japanese jurist, came days after Mr. Trump joined Xi Jinping of China and Vladimir V. Putin of Russia in criticizing the court during a historic three-way meeting at the APEC forum in Shenzhen, China.

The Trump administration last month imposed financial sanctions on the court, potentially constraining its ability to carry out daily operations. Washington has also imposed sanctions on Judge Akane, who helped issue arrest warrants for Mr. Putin and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel. The court prosecutes those accused of war crimes, genocide and other criminal acts.

Japan contributes about one-sixth of the court’s roughly $213 million budget, more than any other country. Ms. Takaichi said on Tuesday that Japan would offer its 2027 contribution early — by the end of this year — in a show of support, after a request from Judge Akane. While she did not reveal the size of the contribution, experts said it would likely be about $33 million, in line with previous years.

Judge Akane welcomed Ms. Takaichi’s backing, telling reporters in Tokyo that the early payment “reflects the high importance Japan places on the I.C.C. and its dedication to supporting the Court as a guardian of the rule of law.”

After the summit meeting in China last week, Mr. Trump, Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin released a joint statement describing areas of agreement, saying in part that the I.C.C. and similar bodies “must not abuse their jurisdiction” against state officials. (Mr. Putin is subject to an I.C.C. arrest warrant over accusations of war crimes in Ukraine.)

Ms. Takaichi, who has built a close relationship with Mr. Trump, is in a delicate situation. She faces intense domestic pressure to forcefully defend Judge Akane, but also appears eager to avoid alienating Mr. Trump. She has raised Japan’s support for the I.C.C. with him on at least two occasions, most recently when the two spoke by phone after Mr. Trump’s meeting with Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin.

Before the Trump administration imposed sanctions on Judge Akane, Japan led a behind-the-scenes effort to urge the Trump administration to avoid blacklisting her, The New York Times reported in August. Japanese officials were concerned that penalizing the judge would undermine the integrity of the international legal system and harm relations between the two allies.

Jeff Kingston, a professor of modern Japanese politics and history at Temple University’s Tokyo campus, said that Ms. Takaichi’s decision to host Judge Akane and offer financial support for the court was a “rare, defiant gesture toward the United States and Donald Trump.”

“Trump from the get-go has been trying to dismantle the multilateral system that Japan relies on,” he said. “For Japan, this is about its own self-interest and about the values that allegedly the alliance with the United States is based on.”

The court will next week convene the trial of Rodrigo Duterte, the former president of the Philippines, on charges of crimes against humanity. The accusations relate to Mr. Duterte’s deadly crackdown on drug dealers and users.

Hisako Ueno contributed reporting.

item.title: Murder Charge Reinstated for French Police Officer in Teen’s Shooting
item.description:
A French police officer accused of shooting a teenage driver dead at point-blank range will stand trial for murder, an appeals court ruled on Tuesday, after an earlier decision to charge the officer with a lesser crime was overturned.

The death of the teenager, Nahel Merzouk, in 2023 inflamed longstanding accusations of police brutality against young men from ethnic minorities and resulted in nationwide unrest. Mr. Merzouk, 17, was a French citizen of Algerian and Moroccan descent who lived in Nanterre, a working-class suburb of Paris.

Tuesday’s ruling, by an appeals court in Versailles, was the latest twist in a case filled with turns. French judges initially ordered the officer accused of pulling the trigger to be tried for murder. His lawyer appealed, and in March 2026 a court ruled that the officer, who in accordance with French legal custom is being publicly identified only as Florian M., should be charged with the French equivalent of manslaughter. That carries a maximum sentence of 15 years.

But then several people, including Mr. Merzouk’s mother, brought an appeal against that decision to France’s highest judicial court. It overturned the charge in June — sending the case back to judges in Versailles for a ruling.

On Tuesday, the Versailles court said in its ruling that there was “sufficient evidence” to charge the officer with murder — which carries a maximum sentence of 30 years. The officer’s lawyer, Laurent-Franck Liénard, said he planned to file another appeal to the higher court.

It is rare in France for a police officer to face criminal charges for excessive use of force during an arrest, even when it leads to death — an issue that international human rights groups have raised for decades. In the few cases sent to criminal courts, often many years later, convictions are infrequent and sentences are usually short.

However, Fabien Jobard, a French political scientist specializing in the police, said that such cases had been increasing — at least in part because more incidents were being filmed.

A bystander’s video of the shooting of Mr. Merzouk’s spread widely, undercutting initial reports about what had happened.

Frank Berton, a lawyer for Mr. Merzouk’s mother, Mounia, said she welcomed Tuesday’s decision and hoped that the resulting trial would “shed full light on this tragedy and ensure that justice is served.”

The Versailles court made its ruling days after the French Parliament passed a bill to offer more legal protection to police officers using firearms during an intervention, which would now automatically be presumed to be an act of self-defense. Left-wing critics have called the bill a “license to kill,” and asked the Constitutional Council to review it before its final adoption.

Ségolène Le Stradic contributed reporting from Paris.

item.title: Woman in Iran Lashed 74 Times for Singing With No Hijab
item.description:
An Iranian woman received 74 lashes on Monday for singing publicly in 2024 without a mandatory hijab, according to her lawyer in comments to an Iranian news outlet.

The singer, Parastoo Ahmadi, 29, had performed without her hair or shoulders covered in a video that spread quickly online and drew the ire of the Iranian authorities, who mandate that women must wear a veil in public. Singing by women is also highly restricted in Iran, and they are banned from singing solo in public.

Ms. Ahmadi and four others connected with the performance appeared at the prosecutor’s office in the city of Qom, where they were lashed, Ms. Ahmadi’s lawyer, Mostafa Nili, told the news outlet, Emtedad, on Monday. They were also banned from performing for two years and from leaving Iran during that time.

A person in Tehran familiar with Ms. Ahmadi’s case, speaking on condition of anonymity out of fear of reprisal from the Iranian government, confirmed that she had received the lashes.

Ms. Ahmadi’s performance in 2024 was at a historic site in Qom. There was no audience, but it was shown live online in what she called an “imaginary concert” in the post of the livestream. The video of the event reached 3.3 million viewers.

Wearing a long, black gown, Ms. Ahmadi sang Iranian folk songs. “I am Parastoo, a girl who wants to sing for the people I love,” she wrote in a caption with the post. “This is a right I could not ignore, singing for the land I love passionately.”

The initial ruling, issued in June, sentenced Ms. Ahmadi and eight others involved with the concert to flogging. It was unclear if the others would be flogged at a later date or had already received their penalties.

News outlets affiliated with the government have reported that Ms. Ahmadi and her colleagues were accused of “offending public decency” and of failing to adhere to legal and cultural norms.

Ms. Ahmadi’s punishment, nearly two years after her performance, comes amid an ongoing government crackdown against dissent. The authorities brutally suppressed mass protests in January, killing thousands of demonstrators, according to human rights groups. Iran has continued to execute and arrest dissidents in the months since the United States and Israel attacked Iran in February.

The war has reduced the political cost of repression for the Islamic republic, said Mahmood Amiry-Moghaddam, director of Iran Human Rights, a nonprofit in Norway. “What used to lead to international outrage, now it barely registers because of attention on the war,” he said.

Women in Iran can be arrested or whipped for not donning the hijab, as Ms. Ahmadi’s case showed, but unveiled women are nonetheless seen throughout the country. In 2022, Mahsa Amini, a 22-year-old Kurdish woman, died in police custody after being arrested on grounds of breaking modesty laws involving the hijab. Her death prompted nationwide protests that were called the “Woman, Life, Freedom” movement. Since then, many more women have chosen to ignore the hijab rule.

Unveiled women have even been seen on Iranian state media and at pro-government rallies amid the war.

But Mr. Amiry-Moghaddam said that Ms. Ahmadi had pushed the boundaries, going further than just flouting the hijab rules, by demanding recognition of fundamental rights. He said that her punishment was part of a broader campaign to spread fear and deter others who were tempted to follow in her footsteps.

“The main threat to the Islamic republic doesn’t come from the United States or Israel,” he said. “It comes from young Iranians who want fundamental change, and that’s why what Parastoo does, as peaceful as it seems, it’s regarded as dangerous.”

Suppression of cultural expression has escalated in recent months, according to the Center for Human Rights in Iran, a nonprofit in New York. The group last month called on governments and the United Nations to pressure Iran by demanding the release of cultural figures being held for their expression and urging an end to corporal punishment such as flogging.

The group highlighted the cases of about eight cultural figures in Iran who had been arrested, detained incommunicado, prosecuted or imprisoned for songs, poems, paintings, books or social media posts in September and October alone. The group also noted that Ms. Ahmadi’s conviction, and those of eight musicians and crew members who participated in the virtual concert with her, were upheld by an appeals court in Qom in September.

“These arrests must be understood as part of the broader and increasingly violent campaign of repression in Iran, aimed at silencing dissent and intimidating entire communities,” said Esfandiar Aban, director of research at the center.

Yeganeh Torbati contributed reporting.

item.title: For China, Jensen Huang’s Return to Nvidia Is a Mixed Blessing
item.description:
The reappointment of Jensen Huang as Nvidia’s chief executive appears to be good news for Beijing: The most influential advocate in the United States for selling advanced chips to China is back in charge after an extraordinary intervention by President Trump.

But the view in Beijing is likely to be murkier. While several Chinese tech executives welcomed Mr. Huang’s return, they also recognized that his hands may now be tied. Lawmakers in Washington are lining up to question him and tighten the rules on chip sales to China.

Either way, the whiplash will give Beijing further impetus in its efforts to wean Chinese companies off U.S. technology and develop their own. And the latest twist in the saga of the world’s most consequential chip company and the man who built it from the ground up ensures that Nvidia will remain at the center of U.S.-China relations.

No company can compete with Nvidia when it comes to designing advanced chips for artificial intelligence, a huge advantage for Washington as it presses to keep ahead of Beijing in the transformative technology.

In the broader competition with the United States, China has exceptional engineering talent, world-class A.I. models, and access to cheap power and vast land for its data centers. It has also repeatedly demonstrated an ability to do more with less.

But China is demonstrably weaker in chips and is still struggling to make enough of them to satisfy domestic demand. Epoch AI, a nonprofit research organization, estimates that smuggled chips account for roughly a third of China’s A.I. computing power, though it says the true share could be considerably smaller or larger.

For China’s A.I. industry and A.I. models, “Huang’s return is good news given its dependence on Nvidia and the importance of American technology,” Lizzi C. Lee, a fellow focusing on the Chinese economy at the Asia Society Policy Institute, said in an email. Beijing, she added, may also see it as “reassurance that practical and commercial interests still carry the day in Washington.”

But Ms. Lee said Chinese policymakers were unlikely to stake everything on Mr. Trump’s good will, given the results of the midterm elections and his lame-duck status. “If anything,” she said, “expect the push for domestic substitution to accelerate after this episode, which already exposed the vulnerability of China’s A.I. ambition.”

Much will depend on Washington, where a debate has been raging about how to approach Chinese access to advanced A.I. chips. That debate intensified in recent weeks after The New York Times reported that U.S. intelligence officials believed that Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman who allegedly had an extramarital affair with Mr. Huang, was an asset working for China’s spy agency.

China hawks and national security officials have argued that the best way to stay ahead on A.I. is to curtail exports of American technology. Mr. Huang and his supporters say it is better to lift restrictions and make China dependent on U.S. chips.

Two key issues for Beijing are whether it will continue to receive Nvidia chips, and whether new rules blocking Chinese companies from remotely accessing chips will persist.

The Trump administration reversed a ban on sales of Nvidia’s H20 chip to China in 2025 and then approved the more powerful H200. Lawmakers disclosed last week that the Commerce Department had approved the sale of more than 800,000 advanced A.I. chips to Chinese companies, including some with ties to China’s military.

Chinese companies had also exploited a loophole until recently. Unable to import Nvidia’s most advanced chips, they rented access to them through data centers in Southeast Asia and elsewhere. That was legal until last week, when the Commerce Department issued a rule clamping down on the ability of Chinese companies to access advanced Nvidia chips through data centers in third countries, and requiring licenses for chip exports to companies in Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil.

A week after his administration unveiled those rules, though, Mr. Trump has helped restore to power their most prominent opponent.

Mr. Trump has framed Mr. Huang’s return partly as a way of keeping him away from Beijing. “Jensen could take the next plane to China, and I guarantee you, they would give him whatever he wanted,” Mr. Trump told CNBC on Monday.

In China, where Mr. Huang’s plight has generated widespread sympathy, some voices have greeted his return as vindication. Chinese officials have dismissed as “smears and slanders” the allegations of espionage.

Ms. Huang, who has not responded to The Times’ requests for comment, was previously at the head of Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center company that bought large quantities of Nvidia chips and is now under federal investigation over accusations that it smuggled those chips to China.

On Tuesday, Asian shares, led by tech stocks, surged on news of Mr. Huang’s return.

China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs declined to comment on Mr. Huang. However, the Global Times, a Communist Party tabloid, suggested that his reinstatement was proof that the spy affair was a “farce” instigated by U.S. media.

On Monday, the same day Mr. Huang returned, the Commerce Department added Megaspeed to a trade blacklist. Mr. Huang is also scheduled to face questions from House investigators and to testify before the Senate next week.

“Jensen is returning to a new political reality for U.S. export controls, which is that there is significantly more skepticism now about having a laissez-faire approach to chip sales all over the world,” said Vivek Chilukuri, director of the Technology and National Security Program at the Center for a New American Security.

Experts widely believe that China is six to nine months behind the United States in A.I. development. Mr. Chilukuri said that if Washington “actually closed the loopholes in export control policy and enforced the rules that are already on the books, that lead could double.”

Tighter controls will only deepen mistrust of Washington in Beijing, where the controversy has been read as further proof that the United States “is not a reliable partner,” said Wu Xinbo, an American studies scholar at Fudan University in Shanghai who advises China’s Foreign Ministry. Washington, he said, could cut off China’s supply chains at any time and on any pretext.

To Mr. Wu, China has been less a protagonist in the Nvidia case and more of a prop in U.S. political drama.

“The Jensen Huang episode reflects the intense political infighting within the United States and China is just the background music,” he said.

Other Chinese analysts warn Washington should not underestimate Beijing’s leverage. China dominates the supply of rare earths and magnets that American factories and weapons makers rely on. Under a trade truce reached last year, Beijing suspended sweeping controls on rare earth exports. But that truce expires on Jan. 10, and its extension could become entangled with the debate over U.S. chip exports.

Chinese analysts also say China is too big a market for American chipmakers to give up. And new restrictions, they add, would only speed up China’s efforts to power its A.I. boom with domestic chips and software. DeepSeek, one of China’s leading A.I. companies, is developing software for chips made by Huawei Technologies, partly as a way to circumvent Nvidia’s own software.

But China’s government and its A.I. companies do not always have the same incentives, said Olivia Shen, director of the strategic technologies program with the United States Studies Centre at the University of Sydney. While Beijing wants its industry to use Chinese-made chips, publicly listed companies like MiniMax and Z.ai want to make globally competitive models, which — for now — can only be trained with Nvidia chips, she said.

Still, Beijing’s ambitions will not change.

“Longer term, they don’t want their access to this important resource to be based on the whims of a particular character in the White House,” Ms. Shen said.

Berry Wang contributed reporting.

item.title: Houthi Attack on Skyscraper in Saudi Capital Wounds 11, Officials Say
item.description:
A strike by Yemen’s Houthi militia on a skyscraper in Riyadh, the Saudi Arabian capital, injured 11 people, the Saudi authorities said on Tuesday, in the latest attack on the city amid a renewed war with the Iran-backed group.

The attack injured four Egyptian residents, three Nepalese and two Indians, along with two Saudi citizens, the kingdom’s civil defense authority said in a statement. The Houthis did not immediately issue a statement or confirm the attack, though the group has repeatedly threatened the financial district of Riyadh and carried out at least two prior strikes that damaged buildings there.

The Saudi authorities did not specify which tower had been hit on Tuesday, but shared an image of the Public Investment Fund Tower, the home of the sovereign wealth fund that has played a major role in Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s efforts to project influence abroad. The tower was damaged last week in an aerial attack by the Houthis.

The group also claimed responsibility for another strike on the financial district this month that damaged a tower belonging to Saudi Aramco, a state oil company. Houthi officials say that their attacks are in retaliation for Saudi airstrikes in Yemen.

Saudi Arabia and the Houthis, who control much of northern Yemen, have been exchanging escalating attacks for weeks, including on energy facilities and airports. Last month, the Houthi militia launched a lethal offensive on an international airport in Riyadh that officials said had killed at least 14 people and injured over 300 more, in what was the deadliest strike in a Gulf Arab country since the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran began in February.

A spokesman for the Public Investment Fund did not respond to a request for comment on Tuesday. Many employees in the financial district have been working from home in recent weeks amid the Houthi attacks.

Last week’s Houthi attack on the Fund’s 80-story skyscraper left scorch marks around its midsection, with windows blown out on about five floors of the building. The strike also damaged buildings nearby, the authorities said, but did not cause any injuries.

Saudi Arabia’s roughly $900 billion sovereign wealth fund is the engine of Prince Mohammed’s plans to overhaul the national economy and reduce dependence on oil. Underpinned by oil revenue, the fund manages high-profile investments around the world, including stakes in major American companies such as Uber and SpaceX, in addition to vast domestic investments in artificial intelligence, manufacturing, sports and entertainment.

In Yemen, where the Houthis are engaged in heavy battles with the Saudi-backed government, the intensified fighting has exacerbated a dire humanitarian crisis. More than 2,200 people have been killed in the conflict over the past few months and nearly 350,000 displaced, according to the World Health Organization.

The two sides have been fighting intermittently since 2014, after the Houthis took over the Yemeni capital, Sanaa, routing the Yemeni government and setting off a civil war. A fragile truce took hold in 2022 but began to unravel in July amid the broader U.S.-Israeli war with Iran.

item.title: Iraq’s Prime Minister Aims to Wrest More Power from Kurdistan Region
item.description:
Iraq’s prime minister ordered a federal takeover of border crossings and oil fields long administered by the country’s semiautonomous Kurdistan region on Tuesday, in a major push by the central government to retake power and resources.

Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi’s move against the powers of the Kurdistan Regional Government comes just days after he scored a symbolic victory against the country’s most powerful Iran-backed militia by sending federal forces into territory that had long been controlled by that group.

Both efforts are part of Mr. al-Zaidi’s risky campaign to assert control across a country long fractured by regional loyalties and roiled by militias aligned with neighboring Iran. His success will hinge on his ability to turn his orders into tangible gains, without triggering armed confrontation between the central government and forces outside its control.

A statement released by the prime minister’s office on Wednesday said he was moving to extend the central government’s control over Iraqi Kurdistan’s borders with neighboring countries, oil fields and oil exports “proceeding from the principle that national sovereignty is indivisible and that protecting Iraq’s wealth is an existential battle.”

The decision came a day after Mr. al-Zaidi launched an investigation into alleged oil smuggling in the region — a form of corruption that experts say most Iraqi political factions are involved in.

The moves followed the same pattern as his efforts last week against the powerful, Iran-backed Kataib Hezbollah, sending forces into the territory they held after he launched an investigation into their alleged oil smuggling.

Mr. al-Zaidi’s actions are largely seen by analysts as political and strategic.

In response to Mr. al-Zaidi’s directive, Iraq’s two main Kurdish political factions set aside an ongoing feud to signal they would resist the initiative.

“The Kurdistan Region is the product of the blood and longstanding struggle of the people of Kurdistan, and any infringement upon its rights and its gains is a red line,” the Kurdistan Democratic Party and the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan said in a joint statement.

The Kurdish minority carved out a semiautonomous region in northern Iraq after the 1991 Persian Gulf War. But in recent years, Iraq’s Arab Shiite Muslim majority has sought to reassert state centralization.

Mr. al-Zaidi’s campaign to rein in Iran-backed militias has provoked concerns that it could trigger internecine conflict, but he enjoys widespread support in the capital, Baghdad, for moving against Iraqi Kurdistan.

“For years, the central government has been chipping away at the financial autonomy and economic viability of the regional government,” said Ramzy Mardini, the founder of Geopol Labs, a Middle East-based geopolitical risk advisory firm. “The danger for the Kurdistan region is that it could retain the constitutional trappings of autonomy while gradually losing the material means to exercise it.”

Iraq’s deepening financial crisis, caused in part by the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran, was likely a reason for Mr. al-Zaidi to assert control over Iraqi Kurdistan’s oil, Mr. Mardini said.

Kurdish leaders have few cards to play against the central government, Iraq experts say.

The Kurds have long had the support of successive U.S. governments, may not be able to count on the Trump administration, which has already pressured its Kurdish allies in Syria to come under the Damascus central government and integrate their forces into the new Syrian army.

“These are also ideas pushed by the Trump administration, in particular his envoy, Tom Barrack, who has said pretty explicitly he doesn’t believe federalism works,” said Renad Mansour, an Iraq analyst at Chatham House, a London-based research institute. “That’s music to the ears of some leaders in Baghdad.”

Iraqi Kurdistan, once seen as a top U.S. regional ally, operated almost as a state-within-a state after the U.S.-led invasion toppled Iraqi President Saddam Hussein in 2003. Iraqi Kurds controlled their own borders and generated revenue through oil fields and oil exports they largely controlled.

But when the region’s emboldened leaders in 2017 called a referendum on independence, the Baghdad government reacted by seizing major Kurdish-held oil fields and halting pipeline exports of oil to Turkey. That pipeline was only restarted this year, when Kurdish and central government authorities reached a deal amid the Iran war, which blocked oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz.

After losing much of its oil revenue, the region’s administration remains vulnerable to Baghdad’s centralization drive. The central government pays public sector salaries, giving it enormous leverage.

Iraqi Kurdistan has been further weakened by a power struggle between its two main parties, which left it without a functioning regional parliament for two years.

Baghdad’s latest moves to cement control will likely unnerve Iraqi Kurds, still traumatized by centralized rule under Saddam Hussein, who was charged by a special Iraqi court with attempting genocide of the Kurds.

A younger generation of Iraqi Kurds, who never experienced Saddam’s rule, meanwhile, have little connection with the rest of the country.

“A generation of Kurds has only really known life under the Kurdistan Regional Government. They don’t speak Arabic. They followed the dream offered by their leaders that they will one day move toward a state,” Mr. Mansour said. “And now their future reality looks very different.”
